chunks.title: Malaria (*Plasmodium falciparum*) - BloomCare Clinical Guidance: Common Diseases & Symptoms
chunks.content:
- **What it means:** A protozoan parasitic infection transmitted by the bite of an infected female *Anopheles* mosquito. In Uganda, *Plasmodium falciparum* is the predominant and most dangerous species.
- **Common Symptoms:**
  - High intermittent fever, chills, and shaking rigors
  - Profuse drenching sweats
  - Severe headache, joint stiffness, and generalized body aches
  - Loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea
  - Severe fatigue, general malaise, and anemia
- **What you can do:**
  - Perform a Malaria Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) or blood microscopy smear prior to starting medications.
  - Maintain vigorous hydration with clean water, oral rehydration solutions, or soups.
  - Use paracetamol for fever reduction while awaiting diagnostic results.
  - Sleep under insecticide-treated mosquito nets (ITNs).
- **When to seek immediate medical care:**
  - Inability to retain fluids or oral medications due to persistent vomiting.
  - Confusion, extreme drowsiness, seizures, or loss of consciousness (Cerebral Malaria).
  - Yellowing of eyes/skin (jaundice), tea-colored urine, or extreme pallor (severe anemia).
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Clinical Guidance: Common Diseases & Symptoms)

chunks.title: Common Cold & Influenza (Flu) - BloomCare Clinical Guidance: Common Diseases & Symptoms
chunks.content:
- **What it means:** Acute viral infections of the upper respiratory tract. The common cold is caused primarily by rhinoviruses; influenza is caused by influenza viruses A and B.
- **Common Symptoms:**
  - Nasal congestion, rhinorrhea (runny nose), sneezing
  - Sore or scratchy throat, hoarse voice
  - Dry or productive cough
  - Mild to moderate fever, headaches, and body aches (more pronounced in influenza)
- **What you can do:**
  - Prioritize bed rest and warm oral fluids (lemon, honey, herbal teas).
  - Steam inhalation or saline nasal spray/drops to relieve nasal obstruction.
  - OTC paracetamol or ibuprofen for body aches and fever.
  - Avoid unnecessary antibiotics: viral respiratory infections do NOT respond to antibiotics.
- **When to seek medical care:**
  - Difficulty breathing, wheezing, or chest pain.
  - Symptoms lasting longer than 10–14 days without improvement.
  - Persistent high fever (>38.5°C) that fails to respond to antipyretics.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Clinical Guidance: Common Diseases & Symptoms)

chunks.title: Cough (Acute & Persistent) - BloomCare Clinical Guidance: Common Diseases & Symptoms
chunks.content:
- **What it means:** A protective reflex clearing secretions and foreign irritants from the airways. Can be dry (irritant/viral) or productive/chesty (with mucus).
- **Common Causes:** Viral respiratory tract infections, allergic bronchitis, asthma, post-nasal drip, gastroesophageal reflux (GERD), or bacterial chest infections.
- **What you can do:**
  - Warm water with honey and lemon (natural demulcent for adults and children over 1 year).
  - Stay well-hydrated to help thin respiratory secretions.
  - For dry cough: soothing demulcent syrups or guaifenesin/dextromethorphan as recommended by a pharmacist.
  - Avoid irritants such as tobacco smoke, dust, and cold dry air.
- **When to seek medical care:**
  - Coughing up blood (hemoptysis) or rust-colored sputum.
  - Shortness of breath, rapid breathing, or stridor.
  - Chronic persistent cough lasting more than 3 weeks (requires tuberculosis screening).
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Clinical Guidance: Common Diseases & Symptoms)

chunks.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) & Heartburn - BloomCare Clinical Guidance: Common Diseases & Symptoms
chunks.content:
- **What it means:** A chronic digestive condition where stomach acid and contents flow backward into the esophagus, causing mucosal irritation and burning discomfort.
- **Common Symptoms:**
  - Retrosternal burning pain (heartburn) often following fatty or spicy meals or when lying down.
  - Acid regurgitation, sour taste in mouth, water brash.
  - Bloating, belching, nausea, and discomfort in upper abdomen (epigastric area).
- **What you can do:**
  - Eat smaller, more frequent meals; avoid lying flat for at least 2–3 hours after eating.
  - Elevate the head of the bed by 15–20 cm.
  - Identify and reduce dietary triggers (spicy foods, caffeine, alcohol, chocolate, fried foods).
  - Use short-term OTC antacids (aluminum/magnesium hydroxide) or PPIs (omeprazole) under pharmacist guidance.
- **When to seek medical care:**
  - Chest pain that radiates to jaw, neck, or left arm (must rule out cardiac emergency).
  - Difficulty or pain when swallowing (dysphagia).
  - Unexplained weight loss or vomiting blood / black tarry stools.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Clinical Guidance: Common Diseases & Symptoms)

chunks.title: Acute Diarrhea & Gastroenteritis - BloomCare Clinical Guidance: Common Diseases & Symptoms
chunks.content:
- **What it means:** Frequent passage of loose, watery stools (three or more times per day), frequently caused by viral, bacterial, or protozoan gastrointestinal infections.
- **Common Symptoms:** Watery stool, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, low-grade fever, mild dehydration.
- **What you can do:**
  - **Immediate priority:** Prevent dehydration by administering Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) solution continuously.
  - Continue breastfeeding and feeding easy-to-digest starchy foods (porridge, bananas, rice).
  - Administer Zinc sulfate daily for 10–14 days for children under 5 years.
  - Wash hands thoroughly with soap and running water before food handling.
- **When to seek medical care:**
  - Visible blood or mucus in stool (dysentery).
  - Signs of severe dehydration: sunken eyes, dry tongue, lethargy, skin pinch goes back very slowly.
  - Persistent diarrhea lasting more than 5–7 days.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Clinical Guidance: Common Diseases & Symptoms)

chunks.title: Burns & Scalds (Thermal & Chemical) - BloomCare Emergency & Clinical First Aid Protocols
chunks.content:
- **First Aid Procedure:**
  1. Immediately cool the burn area under gentle, cool running tap water for at least 10 to 20 minutes.
  2. Carefully remove rings, tight clothing, or jewelry near the burn before tissue swelling starts.
  3. Cover the clean burn area loosely with sterile non-adherent gauze or clean cling film to prevent contamination.
  4. Take paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain management if appropriate.
- **Contraindications (What NOT to do):**
  - NEVER apply ice, ice water, butter, flour, cooking oil, toothpaste, or traditional concoctions (causes tissue hypothermia and severe infection).
  - NEVER pop or rupture blisters (blisters are sterile barriers preventing bacterial entry).
- **When to go to the hospital:**
  - Burns covering large areas (>3% of body surface area or larger than the casualty's palm).
  - Burns on the face, neck, hands, feet, joints, or genitalia.
  - Deep burns with charred, white, or leathery skin, or any electrical or chemical burns.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Emergency & Clinical First Aid Protocols)

chunks.title: Cuts, Lacerations & Bleeding Wounds - BloomCare Emergency & Clinical First Aid Protocols
chunks.content:
- **First Aid Procedure:**
  1. Apply firm, direct pressure over the bleeding wound using a clean sterile pad, cloth, or gloved hand.
  2. Elevate the injured limb above heart level if no fracture is suspected.
  3. Once bleeding slows, gently irrigate the wound with clean drinking water or sterile saline to remove debris.
  4. Apply an antiseptic ointment and secure with a sterile breathable bandage.
- **When to seek emergency care:**
  - Blood is spurting rhythmically or does not stop after 10 minutes of direct, continuous pressure.
  - Deep gaping wounds with fat, muscle, or bone exposed (requires surgical suturing within 6–8 hours).
  - Wounds caused by dirty rusty nails or animal bites (requires tetanus toxoid and rabies evaluation).
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Emergency & Clinical First Aid Protocols)

chunks.title: Nosebleeds (Epistaxis) - BloomCare Emergency & Clinical First Aid Protocols
chunks.content:
- **First Aid Procedure:**
  1. Sit upright and lean slightly forward (do NOT tilt the head back, which causes blood to drain down the throat, leading to choking or vomiting).
  2. Pinch the soft, fleshy part of both nostrils firmly between thumb and forefinger for 10 to 15 continuous minutes.
  3. Breathe quietly through the mouth and apply an ice pack wrapped in cloth across the bridge of the nose.
- **When to seek emergency care:**
  - Bleeding continues for more than 20 minutes despite uninterrupted firm pressure.
  - Associated with significant head trauma, high blood pressure crisis, or difficulty breathing.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Emergency & Clinical First Aid Protocols)

chunks.title: Choking (Airway Obstruction) - BloomCare Emergency & Clinical First Aid Protocols
chunks.content:
- **Adult / Child over 1 year:**
  1. Encourage casualty to cough forcefully if they can still speak or breathe.
  2. If the airway is completely obstructed (unable to cough or speak, clutching throat):
     - Give 5 firm back blows between shoulder blades with the heel of the hand while leaning them forward.
     - If unresolved, perform 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich Maneuver): stand behind casualty, wrap arms around waist, place fist thumb-side just above the navel, and pull sharply inward and upward.
     - Repeat cycle of 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until object is expelled or help arrives.
  3. If casualty becomes unresponsive, lower to ground and commence CPR immediately.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Emergency & Clinical First Aid Protocols)

chunks.title: Medication Safety During Pregnancy - BloomCare Maternal, Infant & Child Health Guidance
chunks.content:
- **Core Principles:**
  - Nearly all pharmaceutical substances cross the placenta to some degree. Self-medication during pregnancy poses severe risks to fetal organogenesis and development.
  - Paracetamol is generally considered the preferred first-line analgesic/antipyretic in pregnancy when used at the lowest effective therapeutic dose for the shortest necessary duration.
  - Avoid NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen, diclofenac, aspirin) particularly during the third trimester because they can cause premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus and impair fetal renal function.
  - Always consult a doctor or BloomCare clinical pharmacist before taking any prescription or OTC medication, herbal supplement, or traditional remedy during pregnancy.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Maternal, Infant & Child Health Guidance)

chunks.title: Essential Prenatal Micronutrients - BloomCare Maternal, Infant & Child Health Guidance
chunks.content:
- **Folic Acid (Vitamin B9):**
  - Essential to prevent neural tube defects (such as spina bifida and anencephaly).
  - Recommended daily dose: 400 mcg daily, ideally started at least 1 month prior to conception and continued through the first trimester.
- **Iron & Folic Acid Supplementation:**
  - Crucial to treat and prevent maternal iron-deficiency anemia, low birth weight, and preterm labor.
  - Take iron with citrus juice or vitamin C to maximize absorption; avoid taking simultaneously with tea, coffee, or milk.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Maternal, Infant & Child Health Guidance)

chunks.title: Pediatric Dosage & Medication Safety Factors - BloomCare Maternal, Infant & Child Health Guidance
chunks.content:
- **Body Weight-Based Dosing (mg/kg):**
  - Pediatric dosages must ALWAYS be calculated based on the child's exact weight in kilograms (mg/kg), NOT estimated based on age alone.
  - Children have immature hepatic metabolism and renal excretion pathways, making them highly vulnerable to medication toxicities.
- **Accurate Administration Tools:**
  - Always use an oral dosing syringe, calibrated dropper, or measuring medicine cup. Never use household kitchen teaspoons or tablespoons, which vary unpredictably in volume from 2.5 mL to 9 mL.
- **Never Give Aspirin to Children or Adolescents:**
  - Aspirin is strictly contraindicated in children and teenagers recovering from viral infections (cold, flu, chickenpox) due to the risk of Reye's Syndrome, a rare but life-threatening condition causing acute liver damage and cerebral edema.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Maternal, Infant & Child Health Guidance)

chunks.title: Infant Fever & Danger Signs - BloomCare Maternal, Infant & Child Health Guidance
chunks.content:
- **Infant Fever Care:**
  - Dress infant in light, breathable cotton clothing.
  - Offer frequent breastfeeds or fluids to prevent rapid dehydration.
  - Never sponge infants with cold water or alcohol (causes shivering and raises core temperature). Use lukewarm water if necessary.
- **Urgent Pediatric Red Flags:**
  - Any infant under 3 months with a rectal or axillary temperature of 38.0°C (100.4°F) or higher requires immediate emergency hospital evaluation.
  - Lethargy, floppiness, inability to suckle or feed, abnormal high-pitched cry, sunken fontanelle (soft spot), or convulsions.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Maternal, Infant & Child Health Guidance)

chunks.title: Over-The-Counter (OTC) - BloomCare Medical Terminology & Pharmacy Glossary
chunks.content:
- **Definition:** Medicines legally authorized to be purchased and supplied directly without requiring a doctor's prescription, deemed safe for self-care when used according to package instructions.
- **Examples:** Paracetamol, low-strength Ibuprofen, Oral Rehydration Salts, antacid chewables, simple lozenges.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Medical Terminology & Pharmacy Glossary)

chunks.title: Prescription Only Medicine (Rx) - BloomCare Medical Terminology & Pharmacy Glossary
chunks.content:
- **Definition:** Pharmaceutical agents that require authorization and a written clinical prescription from a registered medical doctor or healthcare practitioner before dispensing, due to risks of toxicity, misuse, or bacterial resistance.
- **Examples:** Antibiotics (amoxicillin, ciprofloxacin), antimalarials (Coartem), antihypertensives, insulin, controlled sedatives.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Medical Terminology & Pharmacy Glossary)

chunks.title: Analgesic - BloomCare Medical Terminology & Pharmacy Glossary
chunks.content: - **Definition:** A pharmacological agent specifically designed to relieve pain without causing loss of consciousness. Can be non-opioid (paracetamol, ibuprofen) or opioid (codeine, morphine).
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Medical Terminology & Pharmacy Glossary)

chunks.title: Antipyretic - BloomCare Medical Terminology & Pharmacy Glossary
chunks.content: - **Definition:** A medication that reduces fever and resets the elevated hypothalamic temperature set-point down to normal body temperature (36.5°C–37.5°C). Examples include paracetamol and ibuprofen.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Medical Terminology & Pharmacy Glossary)

chunks.title: Antibiotic - BloomCare Medical Terminology & Pharmacy Glossary
chunks.content: - **Definition:** A medicine that inhibits the growth of or destroys bacteria. Antibiotics are strictly INEFFECTIVE against viral illnesses such as the common cold, flu, viral sore throats, or COVID-19. Inappropriate use causes antimicrobial resistance.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Medical Terminology & Pharmacy Glossary)

chunks.title: Antiseptic - BloomCare Medical Terminology & Pharmacy Glossary
chunks.content: - **Definition:** An antimicrobial substance applied topically to living tissue or skin to reduce the possibility of infection, sepsis, or putrefaction (e.g., chlorhexidine, povidone-iodine, methylated spirit).
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Medical Terminology & Pharmacy Glossary)

chunks.title: Contraindication - BloomCare Medical Terminology & Pharmacy Glossary
chunks.content: - **Definition:** A specific condition, disease state, allergy, or factor that makes the use of a particular medication or therapy inadvisable or harmful to the patient.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Medical Terminology & Pharmacy Glossary)

chunks.title: Prophylaxis - BloomCare Medical Terminology & Pharmacy Glossary
chunks.content: - **Definition:** Action, medication, or preventive treatment taken in advance to ward off and protect against disease or infection (e.g., malaria prophylaxis for travelers, post-exposure prophylaxis).
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Medical Terminology & Pharmacy Glossary)

chunks.title: Adverse Drug Reaction (Side Effect) - BloomCare Medical Terminology & Pharmacy Glossary
chunks.content: - **Definition:** An unintended, undesirable, or noxious effect occurring at normal doses used in humans for prophylaxis, diagnosis, or therapy.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Medical Terminology & Pharmacy Glossary)

chunks.title: Paracetamol (Acetaminophen) - BloomCare Pharmaceutical Monographs & Medication Safety
chunks.content:
- **Generic Name:** Paracetamol (Acetaminophen)
- **Drug Class:** Non-opioid Analgesic and Antipyretic
- **Prescription Status:** Over-The-Counter (OTC)
- **Primary Uses:** Relief of mild to moderate pain (headache, toothache, muscular aches, dysmenorrhea) and reduction of fever.
- **Mechanism of Action:** Inhibits prostaglandin synthesis within the central nervous system and blocks pain impulse generation; acts on the hypothalamic heat-regulating center to produce antipyresis.
- **Common Side Effects:** Rare at therapeutic doses. Rarely skin rash, urticaria, or minor gastrointestinal discomfort.
- **Important Precautions & Warnings:**
  - Severe risk of hepatotoxicity (liver toxicity) in cases of overdose or when combined with alcohol.
  - Maximum daily adult dose is 4,000 mg (4 grams) within 24 hours.
  - Check co-administered cold or flu medications to avoid accidental duplicate paracetamol ingestion.
- **Dosage Considerations:** Pediatric dosages strictly require body weight calculation (10–15 mg/kg per dose). Always read product labels or consult a pharmacist.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Pharmaceutical Monographs & Medication Safety)

chunks.title: Coartem (Artemether / Lumefantrine) - BloomCare Pharmaceutical Monographs & Medication Safety
chunks.content:
- **Generic Name:** Artemether 20mg / Lumefantrine 120mg
- **Drug Class:** Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT) Antimalarial
- **Prescription Status:** Prescription Only (Rx)
- **Primary Uses:** First-line treatment of acute, uncomplicated malaria infections caused by *Plasmodium falciparum* in Uganda.
- **Mechanism of Action:** Artemether rapidly clears circulating malaria parasites through endoperoxide cleavage and free-radical generation; lumefantrine clears residual parasites with an extended elimination half-life.
- **Common Side Effects:** Headache, dizziness, anorexia, nausea, abdominal discomfort, palpitations, joint pain.
- **Important Precautions & Warnings:**
  - Mandatory confirmation with Malaria Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) or blood smear before initiating therapy.
  - Must be taken with fatty food, whole milk, or a meal to ensure adequate lumefantrine absorption.
  - Complete the full 3-day 6-dose course even if symptoms resolve quickly to prevent drug resistance and recrudescence.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Pharmaceutical Monographs & Medication Safety)

chunks.title: Amoxicillin - BloomCare Pharmaceutical Monographs & Medication Safety
chunks.content:
- **Generic Name:** Amoxicillin (as trihydrate)
- **Drug Class:** Beta-lactam / Aminopenicillin Antibiotic
- **Prescription Status:** Prescription Only (Rx)
- **Primary Uses:** Bacterial infections of the ear, nose, throat, respiratory tract (bronchitis, pneumonia), skin, and urinary tract. Ineffective against viral infections (common cold, flu).
- **Mechanism of Action:** Inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), leading to bacterial cell lysis.
- **Common Side Effects:** Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, mild skin rash.
- **Important Precautions & Warnings:**
  - Contraindicated in patients with known penicillin or beta-lactam allergies due to risk of anaphylaxis.
  - Complete the full prescribed course to prevent antimicrobial resistance.
  - Report watery or persistent bloody diarrhea immediately (risk of *C. difficile*).
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Pharmaceutical Monographs & Medication Safety)

chunks.title: Ibuprofen - BloomCare Pharmaceutical Monographs & Medication Safety
chunks.content:
- **Generic Name:** Ibuprofen
- **Drug Class:** Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drug (NSAID)
- **Prescription Status:** Over-The-Counter (OTC) for lower strengths; Prescription for higher strengths
- **Primary Uses:** Relief of pain, inflammatory symptoms (arthritis, muscular strains, dental pain), and fever reduction.
- **Mechanism of Action:** Reversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase-1 and 2 (COX-1 and COX-2) enzymes, decreasing prostaglandin synthesis.
- **Common Side Effects:** Dyspepsia, gastric irritation, nausea, dizziness, fluid retention.
- **Important Precautions & Warnings:**
  - Always take with or immediately after food to minimize gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding.
  - Avoid in patients with active peptic ulcers, severe renal impairment, or uncontrolled hypertension.
  - Avoid in third trimester of pregnancy due to premature closure of ductus arteriosus.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Pharmaceutical Monographs & Medication Safety)

chunks.title: Omeprazole - BloomCare Pharmaceutical Monographs & Medication Safety
chunks.content:
- **Generic Name:** Omeprazole
- **Drug Class:** Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI)
- **Prescription Status:** OTC / Prescription depending on pack size and indication
- **Primary Uses:** Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), acid reflux, heartburn, peptic ulcer disease, and stomach protection during NSAID therapy.
- **Mechanism of Action:** Irreversibly inhibits the gastric H+/K+-ATPase enzyme system in gastric parietal cells, significantly suppressing basal and stimulated acid secretion.
- **Common Side Effects:** Headache, abdominal pain, constipation, flatulence, nausea.
- **Important Precautions & Warnings:**
  - Take 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast for optimal acid suppression.
  - Swallow whole; do not crush or chew delayed-release enteric-coated capsules or tablets.
  - Long-term continuous use requires clinical monitoring for magnesium deficiency and bone density.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Pharmaceutical Monographs & Medication Safety)

chunks.title: Cetirizine - BloomCare Pharmaceutical Monographs & Medication Safety
chunks.content:
- **Generic Name:** Cetirizine Hydrochloride
- **Drug Class:** Second-Generation Non-Sedating Antihistamine
- **Prescription Status:** Over-The-Counter (OTC)
- **Primary Uses:** Symptomatic relief of allergic rhinitis (sneezing, runny nose, itchy watery eyes), allergic skin conditions, and urticaria (hives).
- **Mechanism of Action:** Competitively antagonizes peripheral H1 histamine receptors, reducing histamine-induced vascular permeability and pruritus.
- **Common Side Effects:** Mild somnolence (fatigue), dry mouth, mild headache. Much lower sedation compared to first-generation antihistamines (chlorpheniramine).
- **Important Precautions & Warnings:**
  - Caution when driving or operating machinery if drowsiness occurs.
  - Dose adjustment required in patients with moderate to severe renal impairment.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Pharmaceutical Monographs & Medication Safety)

chunks.title: Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) + Zinc Sulfate - BloomCare Pharmaceutical Monographs & Medication Safety
chunks.content:
- **Generic Name:** Low-Osmolarity Oral Rehydration Salts with Zinc Sulfate
- **Drug Class:** Electrolyte Replenisher & Micronutrient Supplement
- **Prescription Status:** Over-The-Counter (OTC)
- **Primary Uses:** Prevention and treatment of dehydration caused by acute diarrhea or vomiting in children and adults; recommended by WHO/UNICEF.
- **Mechanism of Action:** Sodium-glucose co-transport mechanism promotes water and electrolyte reabsorption across the intestinal brush border. Zinc shortens diarrhea duration, reduces stool volume, and speeds mucosal recovery.
- **Common Side Effects:** Generally well-tolerated. Vomiting may occur if administered too rapidly.
- **Important Precautions & Warnings:**
  - Dissolve exactly 1 ORS sachet in 1 liter of clean drinking water (never mix with juice, milk, or boiling water).
  - Administer in small, frequent sips using a clean cup or spoon.
  - Zinc supplementation should continue for 10 to 14 consecutive days even after diarrhea resolves.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Pharmaceutical Monographs & Medication Safety)

chunks.title: Malaria Prevention & Vector Control - BloomCare Preventive Healthcare, Immunization & Nutrition
chunks.content:
- **Insecticide-Treated Mosquito Nets (ITNs):**
  - Consistently sleep under long-lasting insecticide-treated mosquito nets every night, especially for young children and pregnant women.
- **Environmental Management:**
  - Eliminate stagnant water collections around residential compounds (discarded tires, uncovered water barrels, plastic containers) to disrupt mosquito breeding cycles.
  - Install window and door screens, and wear light-colored long sleeves in the evening and early morning hours.
- **Intermittent Preventive Treatment in Pregnancy (IPTp):**
  - Pregnant mothers in endemic regions of Uganda should receive sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) starting from the second trimester as directed by antenatal clinics.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Preventive Healthcare, Immunization & Nutrition)

chunks.title: Routine Vaccination & Immunization - BloomCare Preventive Healthcare, Immunization & Nutrition
chunks.content:
- **Childhood Immunization (UNEPI Schedule):**
  - BCG (Tuberculosis) and Hepatitis B at birth.
  - Polio (bOPV/IPV) and Pentavalent (DTP-HepB-Hib) at 6, 10, and 14 weeks.
  - Rotavirus and Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine (PCV).
  - Measles-Rubella vaccine at 9 months and booster at 18 months.
- **Adult Vaccines:**
  - Tetanus toxoid booster every 10 years or following deep contaminated wounds.
  - Annual Influenza vaccine, especially for elderly individuals, chronic disease patients, and healthcare workers.
  - Hepatitis B vaccine complete 3-dose series for unimmunized adults.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Preventive Healthcare, Immunization & Nutrition)

chunks.title: Balanced Nutrition & Immune System Support - BloomCare Preventive Healthcare, Immunization & Nutrition
chunks.content:
- **Key Immune Micronutrients:**
  - **Vitamin C:** Powerful antioxidant supporting phagocytic cells and skin barrier function (found in oranges, guavas, bell peppers, tomatoes).
  - **Zinc:** Essential for normal development and function of immune cells; reduces duration of common viral infections (found in legumes, nuts, eggs, whole grains).
  - **Vitamin D:** Modulates innate and adaptive immune responses (obtained through sunlight exposure and dietary sources like fortified dairy and oily fish).
- **Hydration:**
  - Consume at least 2 to 3 liters of clean, boiled, or purified water daily to support metabolic function, lymphatic circulation, and mucosal membrane integrity.
chunks.source_name: BloomCare Medical Knowledge Base (BloomCare Preventive Healthcare, Immunization & Nutrition)

chunks.content:

chunks.title: Term: Antiseptic
chunks.content:
Medical Term: antiseptic
Definition: A substance applied to living tissue/skin to reduce the risk of infection or sepsis.

chunks.content:

Definition: A specific condition or factor that makes a particular treatment or medication inadvisable.

chunks.title: Term: Prophylaxis
chunks.content:
Medical Term: prophylaxis
Definition: Treatment or action taken to prevent disease rather than cure an active illness.

chunks.title: Term: Adverse_Effect
